In a statement on Saturday, the US State Department saidChinawas seeking to deny Filipino fishermen access to the area surrounding the Scarborough Reef, near the island of Luzon. In recent weeks,tensionshave flared in the South China Sea, after Chinese ships fired water cannon on Filipino fishing vessels near the Scarborough Shoal. The area has been claimed by both China and the Philippines as each country’s sovereign territory, in a decades-long dispute. headlines.full_text: A beat written in blood across Gaza, Lebanon, Yemen, and Iran TEHRAN — 28 years ago today, Iranian reporter Mahmoud Saremi radioed his newsroom from the Iranian consulate in Mazar-i-Sharif as Taliban fighters came through the gate. He identified himself, reported that the city had fallen, and asked what he should do next. Hours later he was dead, along with eight Iranian diplomats. TEHRAN — 28 years ago today, Iranian reporter Mahmoud Saremi radioed his newsroom from the Iranian consulate in Mazar-i-Sharif as Taliban fighters came through the gate. He identified himself, reported that the city had fallen, and asked what he should do next. Hours later he was dead, along with eight Iranian diplomats. Iran has marked August 8 as Journalists’ Day ever since, a date built around one man’s last dispatch. This year it does not need to reach back three decades to find its meaning. The years since October 2023 have supplied enough. The deadliest beat on earth Gaza has become, by any independent count, the most dangerous place on the planet to hold a camera or a notebook, inside Israel’s continuous genocidal campaign of aggression. The Committee to Protect Journalists puts the regional toll above 260 journalists and media workers, more than 200 of them Palestinians killed in Gaza alone, making Israel responsible for more journalist deaths than any government CPJ has recorded since 1992. Anas al-Sharif kept filing from the north until a strike near Al-Shifa Hospital killed him and five colleagues inside a tent marked Press. Hossam Shabat died in his car in Jabalia. headlines.full_text: Scale of devastation shocks US city's fire-seasoned residents One Spokane resident tells the BBC she realised the immense danger when she heard the fire had jumped over the river. Last year, Chris Matthews was forced to flee with his family of five after a brushfire threatened their home in Spokane, Washington. That evacuation lasted only a few hours. So when an ominous column of dark smoke raced towards him last Saturday, and he and his family were evacuated again, he expected he'd be back home soon. Instead, he returned to find nothing but smouldering ruins. "All of us thought we were going to be able to get back to our houses," he recalls. "And we didn't think it'd be a situation where we were going to lose our homes or anything like that." Smoke and fires are a normal occurrence here in the US Pacific Northwest every summer, as residents wait for the autumn rains to arrive. Small evacuations are not unexpected. But the scale of this year's fires in Spokane is unprecedented. Kira Townsend, 39, says she realised the immense danger when word came that the fire had jumped over the river, which normally acts as a barrier protecting the city from fires. "It's never jumped the river like that, and just roared up the hill that fast," she says. Nearly a quarter of the city population – 65,000 people – were forced to evacuate since the fires began. For those whose homes did not burn down, officials say it may be weeks before it is safe to return to their neighbourhoods. Miraculously, there have been no deaths or major injuries reported from the fires. Matthew Kincanon, 31, fled for his life as the fire entered his neighbourhood of Prosperity Lane on Saturday
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article uses personal, tragic stories of residents who lost their homes to elicit sympathy and emphasize the scale of devastation.

It is also a National Disgrace." headlines.full_text: Four killed in helicopter crash in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro Three Colombian tourists are among the victims of Saturday's crash on mountainside forest of Tijuca National Park. Save Share At least four people have been killed in a helicopter crash in the Brazilian city ofRio de Janeiro, according to a statement from the Colombian consul in the country. Saturday’s crash involved a pilot and three Colombian women who were members of the same family. They were reportedly on a sightseeing flight over Tijuca National Park, a densely forested, mountainous area on the edge of the city. In the aftermath of the crash, Rio de Janeiro Mayor Eduardo Cavaliere called for more oversight ofhelicopter flights, a popular tourist activity. He even suggested such flights could be suspended “for a week or two”, as new safety measures are implemented. “My solidarity to the families of the victims of the helicopter accident that happened today near Vista Chinesa within the Tijuca National Park,” Cavaliere said in a social media post. He added that he had been in contact with Brazil’s National Civil Aviation Agency, ANAC. “City Hall has requested that ANAC take immediate action to intensify oversight and ensure safety in helicopter flights that are circulating with increasing frequency in our city,” Cavaliere explained. “We place the entire apparatus of City Hall at the disposal of ANAC to support the measures and actions that may be necessary.” The crash took place near Vista Chinesa, a lookout point crowned by a small bamboo pagoda. headlines.full_text: Crews recover 19 bodies from rubble of destroyed Gaza building More than 8,000 people remain missing amid rubble in Gaza, with recovery efforts hindered by lack of heavy machinery. Save Share Nineteen bodies, most of them women and children, have been recovered from under the rubble of a destroyed residential building in Gaza City, Gaza’s civil defence said in a statement. The recovery, which concluded on Saturday, is the latest in a slow, largely manual campaign to retrieve the dead from beneath Gaza’s ruins. Such efforts are hampered by a chronic shortage of the heavy machinery needed to clear broken concrete. Mohammed Abu Dan, who oversees recovery efforts, said that work had ended at the “Karam” building in Gaza’s western area after four consecutive days of searching. Specialised medics and civil defence crews would now move to a new site elsewhere in Gaza City, he said, to resume search operations. Civil defence officials have repeatedly said crews are relying on rudimentary tools and exhausting manual labour in the absence of heavy equipment capable of shifting the concrete slabs left behind byIsraeli strikes. Gaza’s Health Ministry says more than 8,000 people remain missing under rubble across the territory. Since the ceasefire took hold on October 11 last year, at least 1,254 people have been killed, 4,121 wounded and 804 bodies recovered from rubble, according to the ministry’s latest count. The overall death toll since October 2023 stands at more than 73,300, with more than 174,000 wounded. According to the ministry’s data, in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup North, the enemy lost up to 240 personnel; as a result of actions by Battlegroup West, over 210; Battlegroup South, up to 210; Battlegroup Center, over 335; Battlegroup East, over 350; and Battlegroup Dnepr grouping, up to 30 military personnel. US Senate passes Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill The US Senate has voted overwhelmingly to pass an anti-Russian sanctions bill authored by deceased Senator Lindsey Graham
Read Full Article at RT.com The US Senate has approved a bill allowing President Donald Trump to impose 100% tariffs on the largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas. Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. Typhoon season in the western Pacific

Read Full Article at RT.com A powerful typhoon battered Japan’s southern island of Okinawa on Saturday, knocking out power to more than 50,000 buildings and injuring six people before continuing toward China. Five elderly people in Okinawa suffered non-life-threatening injuries, while another person was injured in Kagoshima prefecture, according to local officials. Nearly 39,000 buildings in Kagoshima and more than 12,000 in Okinawa were without electricity. The typhoon, named Dolphin, brought maximum sustained winds of 162 kilometers per hour (101 mph), with gusts reaching 216 kph (134 mph). The storm also disrupted travel, with major Japanese airlines canceling flights to and from Okinawa. On Friday, local authorities ordered nearly 260,000 residents in Kagoshima and Okinawa to evacuate as the storm approached, warning of violent winds, heavy rain and high waves. Dolphin is expected to weaken as it moves toward China, where the typhoon emergency response has been raised to Level III, signaling a heightened state of preparedness, and the storm has been classified as an orange-category typhoon. Landfall is forecast between Zhoushan in Zhejiang province and Fuding in Fujian province between late Sunday and early Monday. Chinese authorities have suspended port operations and ferry services in affected coastal areas, while some schools and tourist sites have also been closed. Heavy rain of up to 400 mm is forecast in parts of eastern China, raising the risk of flooding and landslides. RT News App © Autonom

Thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire in a remote part of western Canada spread rapidly, doubling in size since it was first detected on Friday. The Bald Range fire now occupies more than 36 sq miles (95 sq km) across the Summerland and Okanagan-Similkameen districts of British Columbia, according to the BC Wildfire Service. The fire remained "out of control" as of Saturday morning. The district of Summerland, which has a population of around 12,000, was ordered to evacuate. The power went out across the area, officials said early Saturday. Hundreds of residents living in Summerland care facilities, including senior housing, were being relocated to safer areas, according to Interior Health, a publicly funded health authority in BC. "Throughout the night and into this morning, first responders, BC Wildfire Service crews, [Royal Canadian Mounted Police] officers, emergency management teams, and local communities worked tirelessly to keep people safe and fight the fire near Summerland," BC Premier David Eby said on social media. headlines.full_text: Trump Signs New Executive Orders To Restrict Automatic US Citizenship For Children Born In America Donald Trump signed two new executive orders seeking to limit birthright citizenship in the US, focusing on specific categories and birth tourism, after the Supreme Court previously rejected his attempt. Washington:President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is once more trying to limit the number of people who are born in the country who can become American citizens, in a sign that even after his first attempt at limiting birthright citizenship was rejected by the Supreme Court, he's ready to try again. The president said he was signing two executive actions on immigration, including one limiting the number of people eligible for U.S. citizenship after being born in the United States. The written executive order released later Thursday was narrower in scope than the previous one shot down by the Supreme Court and appeared to focus on restricting automatic citizenship to specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations as well as anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States. It also aimed to restrict birthright citizenship to anyone whose parents “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship." A second order seeks to curb what Trump called “birth tourism” by increasing restrictions on visitors to the U.S. who want to obtain visas to give birth while in the country. Trump said he thought his latest actions would be constitutional. “I thought we were going to win it at the Supreme Court. Unfortunately, we had a bad decision, very unfair decision. Our country suffers because of it and we’re ending it a different way,” Trump said. In June, the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s previous efforts

In a bid to address "the concerning rise in serious and fatal accidents" involving the motorised vehicles, it is now mandatory for riders to wear a helmet and high-vis vest on public roads. Those who don't face fines of €135 (£129) for failing to wear an approved helmet, and smaller fines of €35 (£30) for not wearing a vest or retro-reflectors. The regulations also cover other electric transportation devices, such as electric unicycles and hoverboards. Official figures show that around 1,100 people were injured in e-scooter accidents in Paris last year, a rise of 33% on the year before. headlines.full_text: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope The country is home to some of the world's most unique species - but it is losing them at an alarming rate. "Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat. Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement. Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater. Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain. As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival. Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency. This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change. Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion. headlines.full_text: War, terror, diplomacy: What if Israel takes Al-Aqsa Mosque? Reports from Jerusalem suggest that Israeli authorities are taking over one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. If they do, experts say anything could happen, from war to terrorism to ending diplomatic ties. The statement issued after this week's meeting in Jordan was blunt about what might happen next. Israeli infringements on one of Islam's holiest sites, theAl-Aqsa Mosquein east Jerusalem, could lead to "a religious conflict with repercussions that will extend beyond the region and threaten regional and international peace and security," the foreign ministers of 10 countries belonging to the Arab Leaguesaid after Wednesday's emergency meetingin Amman, Jordan. The statement was also signed by ministers from Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, and Malaysia. Jordan's foreign minister called the meeting because of mounting evidence that the Israeli government is surreptitiously changing a decades-old agreement meant to ensure intercommunal peace at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, an area of great religious significance to Muslims, Jews, and Christians. headlines.full_text:
Scientists create viruses with AI US researchers have used artificial intelligence to design and create functional viruses that do not exist in nature for the first time
Read Full Article at RT.com US scientists have used artificial intelligence (AI) to create functional viruses that do not exist in nature for the first time, demonstrating a capability that researchers say could advance medicine but also pose serious biosecurity risks. Researchers at Stanford University and the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard used AI to design thousands of complete viral genomes, according to a study published in Science on Thursday. Nearly 300 of the designs were chemically synthesized and tested in laboratories, producing 16 viable viruses. The viruses were bacteriophages – organisms that infect bacteria rather than humans – and were based on a naturally occurring phage known as ΦX174. Some of the AI-designed versions proved more effective than natural phages at killing strains of E. coli that had developed resistance. AI had previously been used extensively to design individual genes and proteins, but the researchers said this was the first demonstration that generative models could design an entire functional viral genome. Fatemeh Vafaee, a biotechnology professor at the University of New South Wales, stressed that the phages posed no danger to humans but said the capability raised future security concerns. “It’s less ‘should we worry about this virus’ and more ‘AI can now do this at all’,”she told Al Jazeera, calling for stronger oversight. Experts noted, however, that designing dangerous human pathogens remains far more difficult than creating relatively simple bacteriophages.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article presents a balanced view of the potential risks and benefits of AI-designed viruses, but downplays the severity of the biosecurity risks by stating that designing dangerous human pathogens remains far more difficult than creating bacteriophages.

Aerial video captures the sprawling 2,000-year-old reservoirs that once supplied Jerusalem with water and are now at the center of a dispute over preservation, heritage and sovereignty. (Video by Yehoshua Sigala.) Built more than 2,000 years ago to supply Jerusalem with water, Solomon's Pools have become the center of a modern political dispute, with officials from the nearby Israeli town of Efrat accusing the Palestinian Authority of allowing thehistoric siteto deteriorate after it was placed under Ramallah's jurisdiction following the 1993 Oslo Accords. Most archaeologists date the construction of Solomon's Pools, three ancient reservoirs located between Efrat and Bethlehem, south of Israel's capital, to the Hasmonean period in the second century B.C. The reservoirs were built tosupply waterto Jerusalem during the Second Temple period. Herod the Great (37–4 B.C.) later expanded the system to provide water to his palace-fortress at Herodium. "Solomon's Pools are not only the history of theJewish peoplein the Land of Israel and the source of Jerusalem's living water, but also the future of Efrat in our ability to exercise our sovereignty, preserve Efrat's development space and sustain tourism for all religions in the area between Jerusalem and Hebron," Dovi Shefler, mayor of Efrat, told Fox News Digital. Alappuzha, Keralam:Michael Boulos, businessman and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, paid an unannounced visit to Alappuzha on Saturday, enjoying a houseboat cruise amidst heavy monsoon rains along the backwaters. Welcoming him to the region, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor shared on X, "Welcome back to India @MichaelZBoulos! Thrilled to have my friend join me in Kerala." Despite the downpour affecting the district over recent days, Boulos spent time taking in the famous backwater stretch. The high-profile presence generated considerable excitement in Alappuzha, often referred to as the 'Venice of the East' and globally recognised for its extensive network of backwaters, canals and traditional houseboats. The arrival comes shortly before Alappuzha hosts the annual Nehru Trophy Boat Race on August 22, one of the primary cultural and sporting events in Keralam. The water spectacle bears the name of India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. During a visit to Alappuzha in 1952, Nehru boarded a snake boat and subsequently instituted a trophy to establish an official competition upon returning to New Delhi. Boulos, born in Houston and brought up in Lagos, is married to Tiffany Trump. The couple wed in 2022 and had their first child in May 2025. His visit to the backwater hub ahead of the boat race festivities brought notable international interest to the district on Saturday.

Geneva:In a colourful display of soft power and cultural diplomacy, India has gifted five young peacocks to the United Nations Office at Geneva, reinforcing a unique tradition that spans more than a century at the Palais des Nations. The birds -- four classic blue Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus) and one rare white peacock -- were formally handed over by India’s Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva, Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, to UN Geneva Director-General Tatiana Valovaya. The white peacock, whose snowy plumage stands in striking contrast to the iridescent blues of its companions, was particularly noted for matching the signature colours of the United Nations. Valovaya welcomed the new arrivals, describing them as a vibrant addition to Ariana Park. The birds will initially reside in a temporary enclosure for about three months before being allowed to roam freely across the park grounds, joining the existing resident peacocks that have long been a familiar sight to diplomats and visitors. Ambassador Bagchi called the donation a privilege and a continuation of India’s longstanding association with the peacocks of Geneva. “There is a tradition of having peacocks here. We have donated in 1981 and are delighted to be able to continue this tradition,” he noted. The 1981 gift, arranged under then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, involved a breeding pair flown from Delhi Zoo. The gesture draws on the peacock’s status as India’s national bird, a symbol of beauty, grace, and pride.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article highlights India's national bird, the peacock, as a symbol of beauty, grace, and pride, reinforcing a sense of national pride and cultural identity.

headlines.full_text: US Student Visa Approvals for Indians Plunge 62%, Nearly Double China's Decline Amid Trump Crackdown Indian students seeking education in the United States faced a 62% decrease in US student visas issued during the peak May-August 2025 period, significantly larger than the 34% drop for Chinese students, as reported by the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS). New Delhi:Indian students aspiring to study in the United States have suffered a major setback, with the number of US student visas issued to Indians dropping by 62% during the peak May-August 2025 period, nearly twice the decline recorded for Chinese students, according to new data analysed by the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS). The sharp fall comes amid tighter immigration and visa screening measures introduced under US President Donald Trump's administration. The report shows that while F-1 student visas granted to Indian nationals fell by 62%, visas issued to Chinese students declined by 34%.
